title: Hartogs extension across the origin in several variables
statement: Work over $\mathbf C$ [def-weil-field]. Let $m\geq2$ be an integer, and let $f:\mathbf C^m\setminus\{0\}\to\mathbf C$ be holomorphic, meaning represented near every point of its domain by a convergent complex power series in the $m$ coordinates. There is a unique entire holomorphic function $F:\mathbf C^m\to\mathbf C$ whose restriction to $\mathbf C^m\setminus\{0\}$ is $f$. No boundedness or prescribed limit at the origin is assumed.

source.place: WANTED locally: Demailly, Complex Analytic and Differential Geometry, I §3.D, Hartogs extension theorem (3.28), printed p.28, specialized to Omega=C^m and K={0}; uniqueness by continuity and density. Read online https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~demailly/manuscripts/agbook.pdf.

proof.text: Write $(z,w)\in\mathbf C\times\mathbf C^{m-1}$ and put $P=\{w:|w_j|<1\text{ for all }j\}$ and $D=\{z:|z|<1\}$. The restriction $g(\zeta,w)=f(\zeta,w)$ is holomorphic on $\{1/2<|\zeta|<3/2\}\times P$, since $\zeta\ne0$. Apply [lem-sfb-holomorphic-circle-integral-parameters] with $c=0,R=1,\epsilon=1/2$ to obtain the holomorphic function $H(z,w)=(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_{|\zeta|=1}f(\zeta,w)/(\zeta-z)\,d\zeta$ on $D\times P$.

source.place: I §3.A, formula (3.3), printed p.21; I §3.B, formulas (3.8)--(3.9), printed p.22; isolated-puncture specialization of I §3.D, Theorem (3.28), printed p.28. WANTED locally; read online https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~demailly/manuscripts/agbook.pdf

proof.text: Fix $w\in P\setminus\{0\}$. The map $z\mapsto(z,w)$ has analytic coordinates (identity and constants), hence is analytic by [lem-sfb-complex-analytic-function-operations]. Its image avoids the origin, so composition gives an analytic slice $h_w(z)=f(z,w)$ on all of $\mathbf C$. The same node gives continuity, and [lem-sfb-analytic-germ-differentiable] gives complex differentiability at each point. Thus all closed-disc continuity and open-disc differentiability hypotheses of [lem-sfb-cauchy-circle-formula] hold, and its formula gives $H(z,w)=f(z,w)$ for $z\in D$.

source.place: I §3.A, formula (3.3), printed p.21; I §3.B, formulas (3.8)--(3.9), printed p.22; isolated-puncture specialization of I §3.D, Theorem (3.28), printed p.28. WANTED locally; read online https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~demailly/manuscripts/agbook.pdf

proof.text: If $z\in D\setminus\{0\}$, take $w_k=(1/(k+2),0,\ldots,0)\in P\setminus\{0\}$. This is possible since $m-1\geq1$, and $w_k\to0$. Both $H$ and $f$ are continuous at $(z,0)$ by [lem-sfb-complex-analytic-function-operations]. Step 2 gives $H(z,w_k)=f(z,w_k)$; taking limits proves $H(z,0)=f(z,0)$. Together with Step 2, $H=f$ on $(D\times P)\setminus\{0\}$.

source.place: I §3.A, formula (3.3), printed p.21; I §3.B, formulas (3.8)--(3.9), printed p.22; isolated-puncture specialization of I §3.D, Theorem (3.28), printed p.28. WANTED locally; read online https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~demailly/manuscripts/agbook.pdf

proof.text: Define $F(0)=H(0,0)$ and $F(x)=f(x)$ for $x\ne0$. Step 3 makes $F=H$ on $D\times P$, an open neighborhood of the origin. At a nonzero point, a ball of radius less than its distance to the origin avoids $0$, and $F=f$ there. Thus every point has a neighborhood on which $F$ is represented by the convergent power series of $H$ or of $f$. This proves that $F$ is entire and extends $f$.

source.place: I §3.A, formula (3.3), printed p.21; I §3.B, formulas (3.8)--(3.9), printed p.22; isolated-puncture specialization of I §3.D, Theorem (3.28), printed p.28. WANTED locally; read online https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~demailly/manuscripts/agbook.pdf

proof.text: For two entire extensions $F_1,F_2$, their values agree at every nonzero point by the restriction condition. By [lem-sfb-complex-analytic-function-operations] they are continuous at $0$. Along $x_k=(1/(k+2),0,\ldots,0)\to0$ their equal values therefore have limits $F_1(0)$ and $F_2(0)$; uniqueness of limits in $\mathbf C$ gives $F_1(0)=F_2(0)$. Hence $F_1=F_2$. No estimate on $f$ near $0$ was used.
